title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: They led the prisoners straight from Prince Shcherbatov's house down the Virgin's Field, past the left side of the nunnery, to a kitchen garden where a post had been set up. Behind the post a fresh pit had been dug. A large crowd stood around both in a semicircle. It was made up of a few Russians and a great many of Napoleon's off-duty soldiers — Germans, Italians and Frenchmen in all sorts of uniforms. On either side of the post stood lines of French troops in blue uniforms with red epaulets, high boots and shakos.

They arranged the prisoners in the order of the list (Pierre was sixth) and marched them to the post. Drums suddenly started beating on both sides, and at the sound Pierre felt as if a piece of his soul had been ripped away. He could no longer think or understand. He could only hear and see, and he had a single wish: that the terrible thing that had to happen would happen quickly. He looked around at the other prisoners and studied them.

The first two were convicts with shaven heads. One was tall and thin. The other was dark, shaggy and wiry, with a flat nose. The third was a house serf of about forty-five, with graying hair and a plump, well-fed body. The fourth was a peasant, a strikingly handsome man with a broad light-brown beard and black eyes. The fifth was a factory hand, a thin, sallow boy of eighteen in a loose coat.

Pierre heard the French discussing whether to shoot the prisoners one at a time or two at a time. "Two at a time," the officer in command answered calmly. The soldiers' ranks stirred, and it was plain that they were all in a hurry — not the way people hurry to do something they understand, but the way they hurry to get through a task that is necessary, unpleasant and beyond their comprehension.
A French official in a sash came up on the right of the line of prisoners and read out the sentence in Russian and in French.

Then two pairs of Frenchmen went up to the condemned men and, on the officer's order, took the first two convicts in the line. When they reached the post the convicts stopped. While the sacks were being brought, they stared around blankly, like a wounded animal watching a hunter come closer. One kept crossing himself. The other scratched his back and made a movement of the lips like a smile. The soldiers blindfolded them with quick hands, pulling the sacks down over their heads, and tied them to the post.

Twelve sharpshooters with muskets stepped out of the ranks with a firm, even tread and halted eight paces from the post. Pierre turned away so as not to see what was about to happen. Suddenly there was a crackling, rolling roar that seemed to him louder than the most terrible thunder, and he looked around. There was some smoke, and the Frenchmen, pale and with trembling hands, were busy near the pit. Two more prisoners were brought forward. These two looked around vainly at the onlookers in the same way, with the same look, silently begging for protection. They plainly could not understand or believe what was going to happen to them. They could not believe it because they alone knew what their lives meant to them, and so they neither understood nor believed that anyone could take them away.

Again Pierre did not want to look and turned away. But again the sound of a terrible explosion hit his ears, and in the same instant he saw smoke, blood and the pale, frightened faces of the Frenchmen, who were again busy at the post, their trembling hands getting in one another's way. Breathing hard, Pierre looked around as if to ask what it all meant. The same question showed in every look that met his.

On the faces of all the Russians and all the French soldiers and officers, without exception, he read the same dismay, horror and inner conflict that filled his own heart. "But who is really doing this? They are suffering just as I am. Who is it then? Who?" flashed through his mind for an instant.

"Sharpshooters of the 86th, forward!" someone shouted. The fifth prisoner, the one next to Pierre, was led away — alone. Pierre did not understand that he was saved, that he and the others had been brought there only to watch the execution. With growing horror, and with no sense of joy or relief, he stared at what was happening. The fifth man was the factory boy in the loose coat. The moment they laid hands on him, he jumped aside in terror and clutched at Pierre. (Pierre shuddered and shook himself free.) The boy could not walk. They dragged him along, holding him up under the arms, and he screamed. When they got him to the post he fell quiet, as if he had suddenly understood something. Perhaps he understood that screaming was useless, or perhaps he found it unbelievable that men would really kill him. Either way, he took his place at the post and waited to be blindfolded like the others, and like a wounded animal he looked around him with glittering eyes.

Pierre could no longer turn away or close his eyes. His curiosity and agitation, like those of the whole crowd, reached their peak at this fifth killing. Like the others, this fifth man seemed calm. He wrapped his loose cloak tighter and rubbed one bare foot against the other.

When they began to blindfold him, he adjusted the knot himself, because it hurt the back of his head. Then they propped him against the bloodstained post, and he leaned back. Finding that uncomfortable, he straightened up, set his feet properly and leaned back again, more comfortably. Pierre never took his eyes off him and missed none of his slightest movements.

Someone probably gave a command, and eight muskets went off after it. But try as he might, Pierre could never afterward remember hearing the slightest sound of the shots. He only saw the workman suddenly sag against the cords that held him, blood appear in two places, the ropes go slack under the weight of the hanging body, and the workman sink down with his head hanging unnaturally and one leg bent under him. Pierre ran up to the post. No one stopped him. Pale, frightened men were busy around the workman. The lower jaw of an old Frenchman with a thick mustache trembled as he untied the ropes. The body collapsed. The soldiers dragged it clumsily away from the post and began pushing it into the pit.
All of them clearly and certainly knew that they were criminals who had to hide the traces of their crime as quickly as possible.

Pierre looked into the pit and saw the factory boy lying with his knees drawn up to his head and one shoulder higher than the other. That shoulder rose and fell in a steady, convulsive rhythm, but spadefuls of earth were already being thrown over the whole body. One of the soldiers, obviously in distress, shouted at Pierre in a harsh, angry voice to go back. But Pierre did not understand him and stayed near the post, and no one drove him away.

When the pit had been filled in, a command was given. Pierre was taken back to his place, and the lines of troops on both sides of the post made a half turn and marched past it at a measured pace. The twenty-four sharpshooters, their muskets discharged, were standing in the center of the circle. As the companies passed, they ran back to their places.

Pierre watched with dazed eyes as these sharpshooters ran out of the circle in pairs. All but one rejoined their companies. This one, a young soldier with a deathly pale face, his shako pushed back and his musket resting on the ground, still stood by the pit where he had fired. He swayed like a drunk, stepping forward and back to keep from falling. An old noncommissioned officer ran out of the ranks, took him by the elbow and dragged him to his company. The crowd of Russians and Frenchmen began to break up. They all went away silently, with their heads bowed.
"That'll teach them to start fires," one of the Frenchmen said.

Pierre looked round at the speaker and saw a soldier who was trying to find some relief after what had been done and could not manage it. He did not finish what he had begun to say. He made a hopeless gesture with his arm and walked away.
